questions.explanation: The schedule is measured, and the gains were designed offline at chosen points. An online update from the prediction error is adaptation. One linearization is one controller. Exact cancellation is feedback linearization, which this table does not perform.

questions.prompt: The gain is \(2\) at schedule value \(0\) and \(8\) at schedule value \(10\). Linear interpolation at schedule value \(2.5\) gives
questions.explanation: The fraction of the way from \(0\) to \(10\) is \(0.25\), so the gain is \(2 + 0.25 \times 6 = 3.5\). The average of the endpoints is \(5\), which would be the value at \(5\), not at \(2.5\). Reporting \(8\) jumps to the far design. Reporting \(2.5\) reports the schedule value.

questions.prompt: The gain is \(1\) at schedule value \(4\) and \(5\) at schedule value \(12\). At schedule value \(6\) the interpolated gain is
questions.explanation: The fraction is \((6-4)/(12-4) = 0.25\), so the gain is \(1 + 0.25 \times 4 = 2\). Using the schedule value \(6\) as a fraction of \(12\) gives \(1 + 0.5 \times 4 = 3\). The midpoint of the gains is \(3\), which sits at schedule value \(8\). Reporting \(5\) uses the far design.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>two designed gains to interpolate</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">K0   K1</text></svg>

questions.prompt: A weight \(s\) between \(0\) and \(1\) blends gains \(a\) and \(b\). Write the blend in the names \(s\), \(a\), and \(b\).
questions.explanation: The near gain keeps the weight \(1-s\) and the far gain keeps \(s\). The form \(s a + (1-s) b\) swaps the ends. The form \(a + b\) adds the designs. The form \(s(a+b)\) scales the sum and does not recover \(a\) at \(s = 0\).

questions.figure_alt: A row of two gain labels.

questions.prompt: The blend weight on the second gain is \(0.25\), the first gain is \(4\), and the second gain is \(12\). The interpolated gain is
questions.explanation: \((1-0.25)\times 4 + 0.25\times 12 = 6\). Swapping the weights gives \(0.25\times 4 + 0.75\times 12 = 10\). The difference of the gains is \(8\). The second gain \(12\) is the value at weight \(1\).
questions.figure_alt: A curve rising toward a steady level.

questions.prompt: Put these scheduling steps in the order you would do them.
questions.explanation: The points define where you are willing to design. The linear model at each point is the plant that design sees. The measured variable is what the implementation actually has, and interpolation is useless until the designs exist. The check between the points is where a frozen-parameter hope can fail, so it comes last.

steps: Choose operating points that cover the range of the schedule.
Linearize the plant at each chosen point.
Design a linear controller at each point.
Name the measured variable that will select the point.
Interpolate the gains from that measurement, and check a move between the points.

questions.prompt: A schedule of linear controllers has been built. One step is wrong.
questions.explanation: A fast schedule makes the rate of the operating point part of the dynamics. A design that freezes the parameter misses that rate, so the interpolation is not exact at every speed. The other steps distinguish the table from an adaptive update and describe how the table is built.
questions.figure_alt: A curve rising toward a steady level.
steps: Each linear controller was designed at one operating point.
The schedule variable is measured, and the gains are interpolated from it.
If that variable moves quickly, the frozen design is still exact, because each instant has some local model.
A parameter updated from the prediction error, with no measured schedule, is a different mechanism.
reasons: A fast schedule adds the rate of the operating point. A frozen design misses that rate.
A measured schedule is updated from the prediction error.
Interpolation is exact for every speed because the points were linear.

questions.prompt: The difference between this table and an adaptive update is that
questions.explanation: A schedule does not look at the prediction error. An adaptive law does, and it does not need a measured operating condition. Recomputing the table from the error would be adaptation. The recursions are different.

questions.prompt: Which statements hold for a gain schedule?
questions.explanation: Measurement and a family of designs are the definition. The prediction error is the adaptive signal, not this one. One linearization is one controller, with nothing to interpolate.

More than one operating point is designed for.

questions.prompt: Gains \(6\) and \(14\) sit at the ends of a schedule interval, and the measurement is halfway between them. The interpolated gain is
questions.explanation: Halfway is weight \(1/2\) on each design: \((6+14)/2 = 10\). The difference \(14-6 = 8\) is the gap, not the blend. Reporting \(6\) or \(14\) stays at an end. Twice the halfway value is \(20\), which is outside both designs.

questions.prompt: The schedule measurement freezes. The controller you are running is
questions.explanation: A frozen measurement selects one column of the table. It does not start an adaptive update, and it does not cancel a nonlinearity. The design at that point remains defined when the point stops moving.
questions.figure_alt: A curve rising toward a steady level.
options: still a blend that changes with the prediction error
an exact cancellation of the nonlinearity
the single linear design that belongs to that frozen value
undefined, because a schedule needs motion

questions.prompt: Between the design points the frozen linear models are only a hope. A method that re-solves a constrained problem from the current state, instead of blending gains, is
questions.explanation: More points improve a table and are still a table. An integrator on the schedule variable is not a control law for the plant. Wider spacing makes the hope worse. A horizon that starts from the measured state is a different architecture.
questions.figure_alt: A curve rising toward a level below the top of the axes.
options: the same schedule with more points
an integrator on the schedule variable
a larger spacing between the design points
a receding-horizon controller on a model you trust at the current state
